newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr setback inevitable, not ruinous.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr setback inevitable, not ruinous.

text.p: The Australian dollar snapped back about 2/3 cent Tuesday after its latest impulsive push to 82 cents left it overextended when buyers withdrew.

It was the currency's first meaningful retreat since it embarked on a brisk uptrend from 78 cents in early November. But it came as no surprise to dealers who reckoned the dollar was overdue a pullback nor, as yet, was it considered a concern for the medium term bullish outlook.
"It was the correction we had to have," said one at a U.S. bank. "There are bids all the way from US$0.8140 to $0.8115 to cushion it and keep the uptrend on track to 84 cents."
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local currency had recoiled to US$0.8135/40 from an early US$0.8165/70 and US$0.8198/03 late here Monday.

It twice tested a six-year high of US$0.8212 offshore but faltered as buyers, particularly from the options market, quietly withdrew. Japanese profit-taking on AUD/yen holdings, built up over months of samurai issues, snapped US$0.8170 support and snowballed into a stop loss retreat to US$0.8130.
The latter level proved resilient, however, with dealers reporting keen interest to buy dips from corporates and funds who had missed the surge from US$0.8070 last week.

Analysts said the pullback suggested a period of consolidation lay in store between US$0.8130 and US$0.8195, much like last week when it hung around in a US$0.8070/8130 range until breaking higher late Friday.
Most thought the chart background was overwhelmingly bullish for a rise to US$0.8240 and even 83 cents before year-end, but cautioned they would have to reconsider were US$0.8070 to fail at any time.
The currency drew support on the crosses from a sharp selloff in the German mark which helped absorb much of the Japanese profit-taking on AUD/yen.

The German currency was shaken overnight when Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said he favoured a firmer U.S. dollar and dissolved into rout in Tokyo when huge stops were triggered on a break of 1.5600 marks.
That carried the U.S. dollar to 1.5670/77 and the local currency followed to end at 1.2732/48, its highest finish since April 1992, from 1.2609/20 late Tuesday.

The mark's woes helped the local dollar hold up on the yen at 92.95/05 from 93.00/10 Tuesday, but it edged back in trade weighted terms to 60.5 from 60.6. It was further underpinned by the launch of yet another dual currency samurai bond.
The 30 billion yen/A$ issue, on behalf of Anheuser-Busch, was the first in a few days and served to reassure A$ bulls that Japanese retail investors remained keen on higher yielding offshore bonds.

Analysts felt the flow would continue as long as Japanese rates stayed at record lows, which looked almost certain for months yet given subdued economic growth there and a fragile banking system. Data on Japanese GDP today showed the economy grew just 0.1 percent in Q3 and inflation was non-existent.
There was a risk of the A$'s yield premium narrowing from the home side, however.

The local press had been whipping up speculation of a cut ahead of today's Reserve Bank board meeting, saying one was needed to relieve the pressure on domestic industry caused by the rally in the dollar.

Analysts, however, thought it highly unlikely the bank would move so soon after the last cut on November 6 and a Reuter poll of 29 economists put the chance of a cut this month at no more than one-in-ten.
On recent practice if the bank does decide to move it will come Wednesday morning, so silence then would suggest no change until the new year, if at all. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
